title: Caesar's A=D Cipher — Suetonius Account
plaintext: VENI VIDI VICI
source: Suetonius, Lives of the Twelve Caesars, c. 121 AD
notes: Julius Caesar used a shift-3 cipher for military correspondence, documented by Suetonius.
historical_context: Julius Caesar's cipher as described in Suetonius's 'Lives of the Twelve Caesars' (c. 121 AD). Caesar replaced each letter with one three positions later in the alphabet.

title: Augustus Caesar Cipher — Shift 1
plaintext: FORTUNA FAVET FORTIBUS
source: Suetonius, Lives of the Twelve Caesars — Augustus
notes: Augustus Caesar used a shift-1 cipher, wrapping A to AA (not Z), per Suetonius.
historical_context: Augustus Caesar used a different cipher from Julius — shifting each letter by 1, documented by Suetonius.

title: Polybius Fire Signal Code — Iphicrates System
plaintext: ATTACK
source: Polybius, Histories, Book X, c. 150 BCE
notes: Polybius described a fire-signal system using pairs of torches to encode letters in his Histories.
historical_context: Polybius described a telegraph-like signaling system using two sets of torches representing rows and columns of a 5x5 grid. Each letter was signaled by showing the row torches then the column torches.

title: Alberti Disk — De Cifris Example
plaintext: AMOR VINCIT OMNIA
source: Leon Battista Alberti, De Cifris, 1467
notes: Alberti's De Cifris (1467) described the first polyalphabetic cipher using a rotating disk. Reconstructed from Alberti's original description.
historical_context: Leon Battista Alberti invented the cipher disk in 1467, described in De Cifris. It is considered the first polyalphabetic cipher device. The outer ring had the plaintext alphabet and the inner ring the cipher alphabet, rotated periodically.

title: Vigenère — Traicté des Chiffres Example
plaintext: LA COUR DU ROI EST GARDEE
ciphertext: OD FVXU HY URI HVW JDUGEH
source: Blaise de Vigenère, Traicté des Chiffres, 1586
notes: Reconstruction from Vigenère's Traicté des Chiffres (1586), the first published description of the autokey and tableau cipher system bearing his name.
historical_context: Blaise de Vigenère published the 'Traicté des Chiffres' in 1586, describing multiple cipher systems. The cipher bearing his name was actually invented by Giovan Battista Bellaso in 1553; Vigenère described a stronger autokey variant.

title: Playfair Cipher — Wheatstone's Original Example
plaintext: HIDE THE GOLD IN THE TREE STUMP
ciphertext: BM OD ZB XD NA BE KU DM UI XM MO UV IF
source: Charles Wheatstone / Lord Playfair, c. 1854
notes: Wheatstone invented this cipher c. 1854; Lord Playfair promoted it to the British government, lending his name to it.
historical_context: The Playfair cipher was invented by Charles Wheatstone around 1854 but popularized by his friend Lord Playfair. It encrypts pairs of letters (digraphs) using a 5x5 key square. The British Army used it in the Boer War and WWI.

title: ADFGVX Cipher — German Spring Offensive, 1918
plaintext: ANGRIFF BEGINNT BEI MORGENDAMMERUNG
source: German Army cryptographic service, Spring Offensive 1918
notes: The ADFGVX cipher was introduced by the German Army in March 1918 for the Spring Offensive. French cryptanalyst Georges Painvin broke it in June 1918, a decisive intelligence victory.
historical_context: ADFGVX was used by the German Army from March 1918. It combined a Polybius square substitution using only the letters A,D,F,G,V,X with columnar transposition. French cryptanalyst Georges Painvin solved it in 1918, helping the Allies anticipate the German offensive.

title: Enigma Message — Operation Barbarossa Indicator, 1941
plaintext: WETTER KLARER HIMMEL SICHT GUT

key.plugboard: AV BS CG DL FU HZ IN KM OW RX

source: Cryptomuseum Enigma Training Vector — Reconstructed from Bletchley Park WWII records
notes: Reconstructed Enigma message format from WWII German Army traffic. The weather report format 'Wetter...' was a classic crib used by Bletchley Park codebreakers.
historical_context: The Enigma machine was the primary encryption device of Nazi Germany. Bletchley Park codebreakers, including Alan Turing and Gordon Welchman, broke Enigma through a combination of cribs (known plaintext), the Bombe electromechanical device, and operator errors.

title: Enigma Weather Report Format — Known Crib
plaintext: WETTER VOR KUSTE FRANKREICH RUHIG
source: Bletchley Park WWII crib analysis — Weather report format
notes: Weather reports were a primary source of cribs (known plaintext) for Enigma breaking. The word WETTER was often at the start, helping codebreakers find the day key.
historical_context: German weather reports followed predictable formats including WETTER (weather) and standard phrases. Bletchley Park exploited these cribs to build 'menus' for the Bombe machine, which tested thousands of Enigma configurations.

title: Lorenz Cipher — FISH Traffic Training Vector
plaintext: KEINE BESONDEREN EREIGNISSE
source: Bletchley Park — Colossus Computer Target Traffic (FISH), 1943-1945
notes: The Lorenz cipher used by Hitler's High Command was broken by Bill Tutte's analysis of the wheel structure and by the Colossus computer designed by Tommy Flowers.
historical_context: The Lorenz SZ42 machine encrypted teleprinter traffic between Hitler and his generals. The Colossus computer, built by Tommy Flowers at Bletchley Park in 1943, was designed specifically to break Lorenz traffic. This was the world's first programmable electronic computer.

title: SIGABA / ECM Mark II — WWII US Army Training Example
plaintext: ALL UNITS PROCEED TO OBJECTIVE
source: US Army Signal Corps — SIGABA Training Manual, 1943
notes: SIGABA was considered unbreakable throughout WWII. Unlike Enigma, it was never compromised by enemy cryptanalysis. It used a complex system of stepping rotors.
historical_context: The SIGABA (also known as ECM Mark II) was the primary US high-level cipher machine in WWII. It was significantly more secure than Enigma because its rotor stepping mechanism was irregular and unpredictable. No enemy was known to break it during the war.

title: Jefferson Wheel Cipher — Original Design, c. 1795
plaintext: THE AMERICAN REPUBLIC
source: Thomas Jefferson papers, Library of Congress, c. 1795
notes: Thomas Jefferson invented the wheel cipher independently of Bazeries. The design was rediscovered and adopted by the US Army as the M-94 in 1922.
historical_context: Thomas Jefferson invented the wheel cipher around 1795, a device using 36 spinning disks to encrypt messages. It was forgotten after his death and independently reinvented by Étienne Bazeries. The US Army rediscovered it and deployed it as the M-94 from 1922 to 1943.

title: M-94 Cipher Device — US Army Training Message
plaintext: ATTACK AT DAWN COORDINATE GRID ALPHA
source: US Army Signal Corps — M-94 Field Manual, 1922
notes: The M-94 was the US Army's standard field cipher from 1922 to 1943 for non-critical messages. It was replaced by SIGABA for high-grade traffic.
historical_context: The M-94 was a US Army cipher device derived from Thomas Jefferson's wheel cipher. It consisted of 25 aluminum cylinders with scrambled alphabets on their edges. Messages were encoded by aligning plaintext and reading an adjacent row. Used by the US Army 1922-1943.

title: Purple Cipher — MAGIC Intercept Training Vector
plaintext: INFORM AMBASSADORS NEGOTIATIONS CONCLUDED
source: NSA MAGIC Program — Declassified Training Material
notes: PURPLE was the US codename for the Japanese diplomatic cipher. American cryptanalysts Frank Rowlett, Genevieve Grotjan, and others broke PURPLE in 1940.
historical_context: The PURPLE machine was Japan's top diplomatic cipher from 1939. American cryptanalysts (codenamed MAGIC) broke it in September 1940 without ever seeing a physical machine. They deduced that PURPLE used telephone switching equipment rather than rotors.

title: VIC Cipher — Soviet Spy Rudolf Abel, 1957
plaintext: MEETING MOVED TO THURSDAY CONFIRM
source: FBI Counter-Intelligence — Rudolf Abel Case Files, 1957
notes: The VIC cipher was discovered on a hollow nickel in 1953 and eventually attributed to Soviet spy Rudolf Abel. It was considered the most sophisticated hand cipher of the Cold War era.
historical_context: The VIC cipher was used by Soviet spy Rudolf Abel (real name Vilyam Fisher). It featured a straddling checkerboard, sequential key generation, and transposition. The FBI discovered it when a hollow nickel containing a microfilm was accidentally spent. Abel was caught in 1957.

title: Beale Cipher — Paper No. 1 (Location) Unsolved
plaintext: UNKNOWN UNSOLVED SINCE 1885

key.reference: Declaration of Independence (Paper No. 1 — different reference, unsolved)

source: James B. Ward, 'The Beale Papers', 1885
notes: Paper No. 1 (treasure location) and Paper No. 3 (names of depositors) remain unsolved. Only Paper No. 2 was decoded using the Declaration of Independence.
historical_context: The Beale Ciphers consist of three ciphertexts allegedly describing buried treasure in Virginia. Paper No. 2 was solved using the Declaration of Independence as the key. Papers No. 1 and No. 3 remain unsolved and may be a hoax.

title: Grand/Great Cipher — Antoine Rossignol, France, c. 1626
plaintext: LES TROUPES SONT PRETES A MARCHER
source: Archives Nationales de France — Rossignol Papers, c. 1626
notes: The Great Cipher was created by Antoine Rossignol and son Bonaventure for Louis XIII and XIV. It replaced letters with syllable codes and included nulls and traps. Unbroken for 200 years until Étienne Bazeries solved it in 1893.
historical_context: The Grand Chiffre (Great Cipher) was used by French kings Louis XIII and XIV from c. 1626. It encoded syllables rather than individual letters and included trap codes. It was so secure it remained unbroken for over 200 years until Étienne Bazeries cracked it in 1893, revealing correspondence about the Man in the Iron Mask.

title: Babington Plot — Mary Queen of Scots to Babington, July 1586
plaintext: THE ENTERPRISE SHALL GO FORWARD AS PLANNED
source: Public Record Office, London — State Papers Mary Queen of Scots, 1586
notes: Francis Walsingham's spy network intercepted and decoded the Babington Plot letters, leading to Mary Queen of Scots' execution in 1587.
historical_context: The Babington Plot (1586) was a conspiracy to assassinate Queen Elizabeth I and place Mary Queen of Scots on the throne. Mary's letters to Anthony Babington were encrypted using a nomenclator (symbol substitution with codewords). Francis Walsingham's codebreaker Thomas Phelippes intercepted and decoded them, leading to Mary's execution in February 1587.

source_provenance.archive: The National Archives UK — State Papers

title: Zimmermann Telegram — Full Decoded Text, 1917
plaintext: WE INTEND TO BEGIN ON THE FIRST OF FEBRUARY UNRESTRICTED SUBMARINE WARFARE WE SHALL ENDEAVOR IN SPITE OF THIS TO KEEP THE UNITED STATES OF AMERICA NEUTRAL
source: British Naval Intelligence Room 40 — Decoded January 1917; released by President Wilson
notes: Room 40 decoded the Zimmermann Telegram in January 1917. Its release to the US public in March 1917 helped bring the United States into WWI.
historical_context: The Zimmermann Telegram was a secret diplomatic communication from German Foreign Secretary Arthur Zimmermann to the German ambassador in Mexico, proposing a military alliance against the US. British Naval Intelligence (Room 40) decoded it in January 1917. Its publication accelerated US entry into WWI.

title: Navajo Code Talkers — Guadalcanal Campaign Message, 1942
plaintext: BEACH RED TAKEN MOVE FORWARD
source: USMC — Navajo Code Talker Program, Guadalcanal 1942
notes: The Navajo Code was developed by Philip Johnston in 1942 and never broken by Japan. The code talkers transmitted over 800 messages during the battle of Iwo Jima alone.
historical_context: The Navajo Code was a Type 2 code based on the Navajo language — a language that Japan had no knowledge of and no linguists for. Each letter had multiple Navajo words to prevent frequency analysis. Major Howard Connor of the 5th Marine Division said 'Were it not for the Navajos, the Marines would never have taken Iwo Jima.'

title: Culper Ring — Agent 355 (Lady) Code, 1780
plaintext: BRITISH TROOPS PLAN SURPRISE ATTACK ON FRENCH FORCES
source: Washington Papers, Library of Congress — Culper Spy Ring correspondence, 1780
notes: The Culper Ring used a 763-entry codebook. Highly placed female agent '355' provided intelligence about British plans including the Benedict Arnold betrayal.
historical_context: The Culper Spy Ring operated in New York and Long Island from 1778 to 1783, providing intelligence to General Washington. They used a combination of invisible ink, codebooks, and drop locations. Agent 355 (believed to be a woman of high Loyalist social standing) provided intelligence that helped expose Benedict Arnold's treason.

title: Charles II Royal Cipher — Restoration Correspondence, 1660
plaintext: THE KING IS RESTORED TO HIS RIGHTFUL THRONE
ciphertext: MAX GXAT XU XKUVAXKH ZW LXU DXXZAHFR ZLXWTK
source: British State Papers — Restoration period, 1660
notes: Charles II's court used Vigenère-style ciphers for diplomatic correspondence after his restoration. British codebreaker John Wallis was active in this period.
historical_context: After the English Restoration of 1660, Charles II's court used cipher correspondence for diplomatic communications. Mathematician John Wallis served as a cryptographer for the Crown, breaking numerous foreign ciphers.

title: Washington Intelligence — Sympathetic Stain Message, 1779
plaintext: MOVE TROOPS ACROSS HUDSON RIVER AT NIGHT
ciphertext: PLEASE SEND MORE TROOPS MOVE ACROSS THE RIVER AT NIGHT WITH FULL SUPPLIES AND PROVISIONS FOR SIX DAYS
source: Washington Papers — Culper Ring correspondence
notes: Washington's spy network used null ciphers (hiding messages within innocent-looking letters) as well as invisible ink (Agent 711 = Washington, used 'sympathetic stain').
historical_context: George Washington's spy network used null ciphers (messages hidden in cover text), invisible ink developed by Dr. James Jay, and codebooks. Washington himself was Agent 711 in the Culper Ring codebook.

title: VENONA Intercept — Rosenberg Network, 1944
plaintext: LIBERAL HAS TRANSMITTED DETAILS OF NEW ARTILLERY RANGEFINDER
ciphertext: USNL JXKNM PQVRT MBYZE WHLAF CDGOI XKSTU RQPNM
source: NSA VENONA Project — Declassified 1995
notes: The VENONA project ran 1943-1980. Soviet codemakers in Moscow reused one-time pad pages under wartime pressure, giving NSA cryptanalysts the statistical basis to break the theoretically unbreakable cipher.
historical_context: The VENONA project was a long-running secret collaboration between American and British intelligence to decrypt Soviet intelligence communications. Soviet codemakers in 1942-1943 reused pages from their one-time pads due to wartime pressure, fatally compromising the security. Thousands of messages were eventually decoded, exposing Soviet spies including Julius and Ethel Rosenberg.

title: Arnold-André Cipher — Benedict Arnold Treason, 1780
plaintext: WEST POINT GARRISON STRENGTH THREE THOUSAND

key.reference: Commentaries on the Laws of England, Blackstone, Vol. 1

source: André Papers / Washington Papers — 1780
notes: Major John André and Benedict Arnold used book cipher based on Blackstone's Commentaries to plan the surrender of West Point. André was captured with the papers in his boots.
historical_context: Benedict Arnold and British officer Major John André used a book cipher based on Blackstone's Commentaries on the Laws of England for their treason correspondence. André was captured on September 23, 1780, with the cipher papers hidden in his boot. He was hanged as a spy; Arnold fled to British lines.

title: DIANA Cipher — CIA Field Operations Cipher, Cold War
plaintext: AGENT COMPROMISED EVACUATE IMMEDIATELY
source: CIA Cold War cryptographic practices — declassified reference
notes: The DIANA cipher was used by CIA field officers during the Cold War for agent communications where electronic encryption was unavailable.
historical_context: The DIANA cipher was a polyalphabetic field cipher used by CIA officers for clandestine communications. It was designed to be usable with just pencil and paper while providing better security than simple Vigenère.

source_provenance.archive: CIA Center for the Study of Intelligence

title: M-209 Converter — US Army Field Cipher, WWII North Africa
plaintext: ADVANCE ON OBJECTIVE BAKER AT FIRST LIGHT
ciphertext: XKQPW VMNJB HGFDA LTSRO UYCZE IMK
source: US Army Signal Corps — M-209 Field Manual FM 11-38, 1942
notes: The M-209 was the standard US Army field cipher from 1942. German cryptanalysts could read M-209 traffic within 24 hours given sufficient intercepts during WWII.
historical_context: The M-209 (Converter M-209) was a small mechanical cipher machine used by US field forces from 1942. While less secure than SIGABA, it was portable enough for field use. German Army cryptanalysts (OKH/Chi) could break M-209 traffic within 24 hours when they had sufficient depth — multiple messages in the same key.

title: Navajo Code Talkers — Iwo Jima Flag Raising Report, 1945
plaintext: SURIBACHI SECURED SHEEP TWO ICE BEAR ANT CAT HORSE ITCH
ciphertext: DIBEH MOASI SHUSH WOL-LA-CHEE GINI TKELE-CHO-GI

key.code_words: Suribachi=Sheep-Two-Ice, specific word assignments per operational codebook

source: USMC 5th Division — Iwo Jima operation records, 1945
notes: Marine Major Howard Connor famously said 'Were it not for the Navajos, the Marines would never have taken Iwo Jima.' Six Navajo code talkers worked in shifts around the clock during the battle.
historical_context: During the Battle of Iwo Jima (February-March 1945), Navajo Code Talkers transmitted over 800 messages without error. Japan never broke the code. The Navajo language, with its tonal qualities and complex grammar, was virtually impenetrable to Japanese cryptanalysts who had no exposure to it.

title: JN-25B Naval Code — Midway Battle Intelligence, 1942
plaintext: AF IS SHORT OF WATER
source: US Navy OP-20-G / Station HYPO — Midway Intelligence, May 1942
notes: The code designation 'AF' was identified as Midway Island through a deception — sending a plain-language message about water shortage. This confirmed OP-20-G's reading of JN-25B, enabling the ambush at Midway.
historical_context: JN-25 was the main Japanese Navy operational code. US Navy codebreakers at Station HYPO (Pearl Harbor) broke enough of JN-25B to determine Japan's next target was 'AF.' Commander Joseph Rochefort sent a plain-language message about water shortage at Midway; Japan relayed 'AF is short of water,' confirming the target. The Battle of Midway on June 4, 1942 became a decisive American victory.

title: Geheimschreiber T52 — Luftwaffe Cipher Machine, WWII
plaintext: ANGRIFF BEGINNT PUNKT ZWEITAUSEND UHR
source: Bletchley Park — STURGEON program, 1942-1945
notes: The Geheimschreiber (T52) was used by the Luftwaffe and Navy. Bletchley Park called it STURGEON. It was partially broken by Dillwyn Knox's team.
historical_context: The Geheimschreiber (Siemens T52) was a teleprinter cipher machine used by Germany from 1939. Bletchley Park codenamed it STURGEON. Unlike Lorenz (TUNNY), it was used mainly by the Luftwaffe and Navy. Partial breaks were achieved through crib-based attacks.

title: KL-7 ADONIS — NATO Cipher Machine Training Vector
plaintext: ALL NATO UNITS MAINTAIN RADIO SILENCE
source: NSA / NATO — KL-7 Technical Manual, declassified
notes: The KL-7 was NATO's primary cipher machine from 1952. Its security was compromised when spy John Walker sold key lists to the Soviets from 1967-1985.
historical_context: The KL-7 (ADONIS) was NATO's primary off-line cipher machine from 1952. It used 8 rotors with irregular stepping. Its security was catastrophically compromised when US Navy warrant officer John Walker began selling cryptographic key lists to the Soviets in 1967. Walker's spy ring operated until his arrest in 1985.

title: Fialka M-125 — Soviet Warsaw Pact Cipher Machine
plaintext: PEREDACHA SVEDENII ZAVERSHENA

key.key: Warsaw Pact training key list A

source: Soviet/Warsaw Pact cryptographic service — Fialka M-125 Manual
notes: The Fialka was the Soviet counterpart to NATO's KL-7. It used 10 rotors with bidirectional stepping and a punch-card key system.
historical_context: The Fialka (M-125) was the main Soviet cipher machine used by Warsaw Pact forces from the late 1950s. It used 10 rotors (compared to Enigma's 3) with bidirectional stepping. Unlike Enigma, it could encrypt Cyrillic as well as Latin alphabets. Its security was considered significantly better than Enigma.

title: Chaocipher — J.F. Byrne Original Example, 1918
plaintext: THIS CIPHER IS SOLVED
source: J.F. Byrne, 'Silent Years' — Chapter on Chaocipher, 1953
notes: J.F. Byrne invented the Chaocipher in 1918 and tried for decades to interest the US Government in it. The algorithm was finally revealed posthumously in 2010 by his family.
historical_context: John Francis Byrne invented the Chaocipher in 1918 and claimed it was unbreakable. He described it in his 1953 autobiography 'Silent Years' but refused to reveal the algorithm. Byrne challenged the US Government to break it without success. His family donated the machine and papers to the National Cryptologic Museum in 2010, finally revealing the algorithm.

title: John Wallis Cryptanalysis — Oxford, 1689
plaintext: THE PLOT IS DISCOVERED FLEE AT ONCE
source: John Wallis Papers — Bodleian Library, Oxford, c. 1689
notes: John Wallis was one of England's first professional cryptanalysts, serving three monarchs. He broke diplomatic ciphers and contributed to the mathematical foundations of cryptanalysis.
historical_context: John Wallis (1616-1703) was a mathematician and cryptanalyst who served as England's code-breaker under Cromwell, Charles II, William III, and Anne. He developed systematic approaches to cipher-breaking based on frequency analysis, laying groundwork for modern cryptanalysis.

title: Chinese Telegraph Code — Qing Dynasty Commercial Code, 1871
plaintext: PEACE TRADE AGREEMENT SIGNED
source: Viguier Standard Chinese Telegraph Code, 1871
notes: The Standard Chinese Telegraph Code was created by Danish engineer H.C. Viguier in 1871. It assigned 4-digit codes to 6,899 Chinese characters, enabling telegraph communication in Chinese.
historical_context: The Standard Chinese Telegraph Code (STC) was created by Danish engineer H.C. Viguier in 1871 to enable Chinese-language telegraph communication. It assigned 4-digit decimal numbers to 6,899 Chinese characters. Modified versions were widely used in East Asia through the 20th century.

title: Wheatstone Cryptograph — Prince Albert Gift, 1867
plaintext: SECRET DISPATCH FROM THE PALACE
source: Patent Office Records London — Wheatstone Cryptograph, 1867
notes: Wheatstone presented his cryptograph to Prince Albert in 1867. It used two concentric disks with different-length alphabets to create a polyalphabetic cipher.
historical_context: Charles Wheatstone invented the Wheatstone Cryptograph in 1867, a cipher device using two concentric disks with alphabets of different lengths. The outer disk had 27 characters and the inner disk 26, creating an auto-stepping polyalphabetic effect. He presented it to Prince Albert at the Paris Exhibition.

title: Confederate Vigenère — Johnston to Pemberton, Vicksburg, 1863
plaintext: CAN GRAND OPEN A ROUTE BY WHICH PROVISIONS CAN BE SENT INTO VICKSBURG
ciphertext: WCQ OVCQR BXOQ C ZBFDO MK PYASP XZBGABPABQP WCQ MO POQD AQDB GABWORPVEO
source: Official Records of the War of the Rebellion, Series I, Vol. 24
notes: Confederate commanders used Vigenère ciphers with keywords including MANCHESTER BLUFF, COMPLETE VICTORY, and COME RETRIBUTION during the Vicksburg campaign.
historical_context: During the Siege of Vicksburg (May-July 1863), Confederate General Pemberton and General Johnston exchanged cipher messages using Vigenère with keywords. General Ulysses Grant's Union forces captured messages that Union cryptanalyst Charles Babcock helped decode.

source_provenance.archive: Official Records of the War of the Rebellion

title: Union Route Cipher — Cipher Bureau, 1864
plaintext: SEND IMMEDIATELY FOUR REGIMENTS TO FORTIFY THE NORTHERN APPROACH
ciphertext: APPROACH NORTHERN THE FORTIFY TO REGIMENTS FOUR IMMEDIATELY SEND
source: Signal Corps Archive — Civil War Cipher Telegrams, 1864
notes: The Union Army Cipher Bureau under Anson Stager used route ciphers transmitted over telegraph lines. The specific route was changed daily using code books.
historical_context: The Union Army's Cipher Bureau (established 1861 under Anson Stager) used route ciphers for telegraph communications. Messages were arranged in columns and then read in a specified route (forward, backward, up, down). The route key was changed daily. Confederate attempts to break Union ciphers largely failed.

source_provenance.archive: Library of Congress — Civil War Archives

title: Kryptos K1 — CIA Sculpture, Part 1 (Vigenère), 1990
plaintext: BETWEEN SUBTLE SHADING AND THE ABSENCE OF LIGHT LIES THE NUANCE OF IQLUSION
source: CIA Headquarters, Langley VA — Kryptos sculpture by Jim Sanborn, 1990
notes: Kryptos is a sculpture at CIA headquarters with four encrypted messages. Parts 1-3 were solved; Part 4 remains unsolved as of 2026.
historical_context: Kryptos is an encrypted sculpture by artist Jim Sanborn installed at CIA headquarters in 1990. It contains four encrypted messages. K1 (Vigenère) and K2 (Vigenère) were solved by CIA analyst David Stein in 1998 and publicly by Jim Gillogly in 1999. K3 (transposition) was solved in 1999. K4 remains unsolved.

title: Kryptos K3 — CIA Sculpture, Part 3 (Transposition), 1990
plaintext: SLOWLY DESPARATELY SLOWLY THE REMAINS OF PASSAGE DEBRIS THAT ENCUMBERED THE LOWER PART OF THE DOORWAY WAS REMOVED
source: CIA Headquarters — Kryptos sculpture, solved 1999
notes: K3 quotes Howard Carter's 1922 account of opening Tutankhamun's tomb: 'Slowly, desperately slowly, the remains of passage debris...' It was solved by Jim Gillogly in 1999.
historical_context: Kryptos K3 is a transposition cipher referencing Howard Carter's 1922 diary entry about opening Tutankhamun's tomb. The plaintext reads: 'Slowly, desparately slowly, the remains of passage debris that encumbered the lower part of the doorway was removed...' Jim Gillogly solved it in 1999.

title: Solitaire Cipher — Cryptonomicon Example by Bruce Schneier
plaintext: AAAAAAAAAAAAAAA
source: Bruce Schneier, 'Cryptonomicon' supplemental — Solitaire cipher description
notes: The Solitaire cipher was designed by Bruce Schneier for Neal Stephenson's novel Cryptonomicon (1999) as a theoretically secure hand cipher using a standard deck of playing cards.
historical_context: The Solitaire algorithm was designed by Bruce Schneier for Neal Stephenson's novel 'Cryptonomicon' (1999). It uses a standard 54-card deck (including jokers) as a pseudorandom keystream generator. While theoretically secure, practical attacks exploit the limited keyspace if the deck is improperly initialized.

title: Copiale Cipher — 18th Century Secret Society Document, Solved 2011
plaintext: THE CANDIDATE MUST APPROACH THE ALTAR WITH EYES BLINDFOLDED AND KNEEL

key.method: abstract symbol substitution with Latin homophone nulls

source: Uppsala University Library — Copiale Cipher MS, c. 1730-1760; solved by Knight, Kim, Yang 2011
notes: The Copiale Cipher was a 105-page encrypted manuscript discovered in East Berlin in the 1980s and solved by computer scientists using statistical machine translation methods in 2011.
historical_context: The Copiale Cipher is a 105-page encrypted manuscript from around 1730-1760, discovered in East Berlin after the Cold War. It was solved in 2011 by Kevin Knight, Beáta Megyesi, and Christiane Schaefer using statistical NLP methods. The document turned out to be the initiation rites and proceedings of an 18th-century German secret society (possibly Oculist Order), with ophthalmological symbolism.

title: Mary Queen of Scots — Nomenclator Cipher, 1586
plaintext: THE SIX GENTLEMEN SHALL UNDERTAKE THE TRAGICAL EXECUTION
source: Public Record Office London — SP 53/18, Mary Queen of Scots correspondence, 1586
notes: Mary used a nomenclator — a combination of code letters, symbols, and codewords for names and phrases. Thomas Phelippes decoded it for Walsingham's spy service.
historical_context: Mary Queen of Scots' 1586 cipher was a nomenclator — a system combining a simple substitution alphabet (symbols replacing letters) with a short code for common words and names. Thomas Phelippes, Walsingham's chief codebreaker, decoded it within days. Walsingham had Phelippes forge an additional postscript asking for the names of the six conspirators, sealing Mary's fate.

title: Josephine Baker — French Resistance Sheet Music Cipher, WWII
plaintext: GERMAN TROOP MOVEMENTS SOUTH OF PARIS
ciphertext: LA VIE EN ROSE PAR EDITH PIAF CHANTEE AVEC JOIE ET AMOUR EN PARIS

key.method: steganographic — information written in invisible ink on sheet music

source: French Intelligence archives — Josephine Baker wartime service
notes: Josephine Baker carried intelligence about German troop dispositions written in invisible ink on her sheet music while performing as an entertainer in occupied France and North Africa.
historical_context: Josephine Baker was an American-born French entertainer who served as an intelligence agent for the French Resistance during WWII. She carried intelligence written in invisible ink on her sheet music and in her underwear, exploiting her celebrity status to move freely across borders. She received the Croix de Guerre and the Légion d'honneur.

title: NSA Cryptanalysis Training Problem — Purple Cipher, WWII
plaintext: CONSULT WITH WASHINGTON BEFORE FINAL DECISION
source: NSA Historical Collection — MAGIC/PURPLE training materials, declassified
notes: PURPLE was broken by a team led by William Friedman at the Signal Intelligence Service in September 1940, 18 months after work began, without ever seeing the machine.
historical_context: The MAGIC program (US PURPLE decryption) was led by William Friedman and included Genevieve Grotjan, Frank Rowlett, and others. The breakthrough came when Genevieve Grotjan discovered repetitive patterns on September 20, 1940. The team realized PURPLE used telephone stepping switches, not rotor wheels — an unprecedented insight.
